A_target.statement:
Let $V$ be a [[Definition:Vector Space|vector space]] and $\map {\operatorname {Sym} } V$ its [[Definition:Symmetric Algebra|symmetric algebra]].
Then for every [[Definition:Commutative Algebra|commutative algebra]] $A$ and [[Definition:Linear Transformation|linear map]] $f: V \to A$, there is a [[Definition:Unique|unique]] [[Definition:Algebra Homomorphism|algebra homomorphism]] $\map {\operatorname {Sym} } V \to A$ extending $f$.

B_source.statement:
Let $I$ be a two-sided [[Definition:Ideal of Algebra|ideal]] of an algebra $T$.
Then:
:$\map {\operatorname {Hom}_{\text {alg} } } {T / I, A} \cong \set {g \in \map {\operatorname {Hom}_{\text {alg} } } {T, A}: \map g I = 0}$

substitutions.the two-sided ideal: the ideal generated by all differences v tensor w - w tensor v

derived.algebra maps killing the ideal: algebra maps out of the tensor algebra whose image is commutative
derived.composition with the universal property: linear maps from V into commutative algebras

object_map.reformulation: Impose commutativity as a relation rather than a hypothesis, so the universal property comes from a quotient.

validity_conditions: The tensor algebra is free on V among associative algebras, so algebra maps out of it correspond exactly to linear maps out of V.
An algebra map kills the commutator ideal precisely when the images of elements of V commute, which for a map generated by V means the image is commutative.
The universal property of the quotient then converts this into the stated classification for Sym(V).
proof_plan: The [[Definition:Tensor Algebra|tensor algebra]] $\map T V$ is [[Definition:Free Algebra|free]] on $V$: linear maps $V \to A$ extend uniquely to algebra maps $\map T V \to A$.
Let $I = \ideal {v \otimes w - w \otimes v: v, w \in V}$, and set $\map {\operatorname {Sym} } V = \map T V / I$.

By the source result, algebra maps $\map {\operatorname {Sym} } V \to A$ correspond to algebra maps $g: \map T V \to A$ killing $I$.
As $V$ generates $\map T V$, $g$ kills $I$ {{iff}} $\map g v$ and $\map g w$ commute for all $v, w$, which holds automatically when $A$ is commutative.

Composing with freeness, linear maps $V \to A$ into a commutative algebra correspond to algebra maps $\map {\operatorname {Sym} } V \to A$.
{{qed}}
